disclosure: Precomputed model-style interpretations of checked-in demo evidence. These outputs never set scores, routes, blockers, approvals, or outcomes.

outputs.summary: Three independent public source families and synthetic consumer language point to a time-bounded confidence-under-pressure moment for Rexona. Commerce progression is positive but modest, and the operating record shows execution is only credible in the four cells that can serve demand.

themes.label: Consumers name the need, not the brand
Execution is narrower than the attention

counterHypothesis.claim: Seasonal heat plus one-off match attention may explain the movement without any brand-specific demand shift; the commerce record is too weak to separate the two.

outputs.summary: Search language persists well beyond a single event window and synthetic consumer routines describe scalp-first behaviour, which supports a durable shift rather than a moment. Claim substantiation and product readiness remain the binding constraints.

counterHypothesis.claim: Interest may stay informational and never convert into a distinct paid hair-care routine, leaving the category with attention but no new demand.

outputs.summary: Visible attention is concentrated in a single creator family and is not accompanied by category search or commerce progression, so the spike does not currently describe category demand.

themes.label: One source family carries the spike

counterHypothesis.claim: Paid seeding, creator novelty, or entertainment value explains the spike better than any deodorant category demand shift.
